topic: Valkey versus Redis: when Redis takeout is practical
purpose: Support a 20-minute technical presentation for platform engineers deciding where Redis takeout is appropriate; supply a prioritized storyline, evidence for speaker notes and caveats
scope: Version and edition boundaries, workload dependencies, operations, migration validation and rollback as of 2026-10-17

facts.statement: Valkey documents Redis OSS 7.2 and earlier as its compatibility baseline; Valkey 7.2.4 forked Redis OSS 7.2.4.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: Valkey is compatible with Redis OSS 7.2 and all earlier open-source Redis versions, as Valkey 7.2.4 is a fork of Redis OSS 7.2.4.

facts.statement: The Valkey migration guide states that Redis Community Edition 7.4 and later produce data files that are not compatible with Valkey.
facts.author: report-revision

citations.quote: Redis Community Edition (CE) version 7.4 and later produce data files that are not compatible with Valkey.

facts.statement: Valkey documents RESP2/RESP3 and connection support for existing Redis client libraries.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: Protocol: Valkey uses the RESP wire protocol and supports both RESP2 and RESP3. Existing Redis client libraries can connect to Valkey without code changes.

facts.statement: Valkey documents support for Redis OSS modules using the RedisModule_ API.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: Modules: Modules written for Redis OSS using the `RedisModule_` API work in Valkey.

facts.statement: Valkey reports redis_version:7.2.4 for backward compatibility; its actual version is exposed separately.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: INFO: Valkey reports `redis_version:7.2.4` in the [INFO](../commands/info.md) output for backward compatibility. Use `server_name` and `valkey_version` to detect the actual Valkey server and version.

facts.statement: The standalone migration examples use Redis 7.2.5 and Valkey 7.2.6.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: The example migration steps are provided for Redis 7.2.5 and Valkey version 7.2.6.

facts.statement: The documented physical migration incurs shutdown/load downtime and requires disconnecting active connections to prevent write loss.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote:
* The downtime to shutdown Redis and wait for Valkey to load the data. 
* Potential risk of data loss on instances with heavy writes. To prevent it, you must disconnect all active connections before starting the migration.

facts.statement: The migration guide describes adding Valkey cluster replicas, promoting one per Redis primary, and removing Redis nodes.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: The first step is to add the required number of Valkey nodes to the existing cluster as replicas. Once the new Valkey nodes replicate the data, one Valkey replica is promoted to be a new primary for each Redis primary. After the migration, the Redis nodes are removed from the cluster.

facts.statement: Valkey 8.0 release notes include aborting transactions on nested MULTI or WATCH commands.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: Abort transactions on nested `MULTI` or `WATCH` commands.

facts.statement: Valkey 9.1 release notes say the Lua scripting engine is statically linked by default.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: Lua scripting engine is now statically linked by default instead of dynamically linked

facts.statement: Valkey 9.1 release notes record extracting Lua scripting into a Valkey module.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: Move Lua scripting engine into a Valkey module

facts.statement: The live Valkey download page lists 9.1.2 as its 9.x release.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: GitHub Release: 9.1.2

facts.statement: The Redis GitHub latest-release API returns 8.10.2, published 2026-09-17.
facts.author: valkey-research

facts.statement: Valkey 9.1.2 declares BSD-3-Clause licensing.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

facts.statement: Redis 8 and later offer a choice of RSALv2, SSPLv1 or AGPLv3; the earlier license boundary differs.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: Redis 8 in Redis Open Source and later versions are available under our tri-license, allowing us to be both source-available and open source software. Our tri-license includes RSALv2, SSPLv1, and AGPLv3.

facts.statement: Redis 7.2.x and earlier retain BSD3; Redis CE 7.4.x–7.8.x use RSALv2/SSPLv1.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: Redis 7.2.x of Redis Open Source and earlier versions remain subject to the BSD3 license. Redis Community Edition 7.4.x to 7.8.x remain subject to the dual RSALv2/SSPLv1 license.

facts.statement: Redis 8 includes RediSearch, RedisJSON, RedisTimeSeries and RedisBloom under the Redis tri-license.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: RediSearch, RedisJSON, RedisTimeSeries, and RedisBloom are now included as integral components of Redis Open Source and subject to the same tri-license. Starting with Redis 8, the version numbers of all included modules are identical to the version number of Redis Open Source they are included in.

facts.statement: The live Valkey Search README documents vector ANN/KNN and Numeric, Tag and Full-text search, indexing Hash or Valkey JSON data. This is a main-branch capability description.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote:
It also provides
support for hybrid / pure non vector workloads including Numeric, Tag, and Full-text searches.

Valkey-Search allows users to create indexes and perform searches, incorporating complex filters.
Users can index data using either **[Valkey Hash](hashes.md)** or **[Valkey-JSON](valkey-json.md)** data types.
The vector queries support Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search with HNSW and exact matching using K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN).

facts.statement: The live Valkey JSON README describes a module for native JSON support; its captured branch is unstable.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: Valkey-json is a Valkey module written in C++ that provides native JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) support for Valkey.

facts.statement: Redis Software Active-Active uses CRDTs and entails different data types plus more complex replication/networking than a database without geo-distribution.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: In Redis Software, Active-Active geo-distribution is based on conflict-free replicated data type (CRDT) technology. Compared to databases without geo-distribution, Active-Active databases have more complex replication and networking, as well as a different data type.

facts.statement: Valkey replication is asynchronous.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: Valkey uses asynchronous replication, with asynchronous replica-to-primary acknowledges of the amount of data processed.

facts.statement: Valkey WAIT does not create strong consistency; acknowledged writes may still be lost on failover depending on persistence configuration.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote:
the `WAIT` command. However `WAIT` is only able to ensure there are the
specified number of acknowledged copies in the other Valkey instances, it does not
turn a set of Valkey instances into a CP system with strong consistency: acknowledged
writes can still be lost during a failover, depending on the exact configuration
of the Valkey persistence.

facts.statement: Valkey documents fork pauses for RDB persistence on large datasets; AOF also forks, with rewrite frequency configurable.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: RDB needs to fork() often in order to persist on disk using a child process. fork() can be time consuming if the dataset is big, and may result in Valkey stopping serving clients for some milliseconds or even for one second if the dataset is very big and the CPU performance is not great. AOF also needs to fork() but less frequently and you can tune how often you want to rewrite your logs without any trade-off on durability.

facts.statement: Valkey documents appendfsync everysec as potentially losing one second of data during a disaster.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: `appendfsync everysec`: `fsync` every second. Fast enough and you may lose 1 second of data if there is a disaster.

facts.statement: ElastiCache only documents engine rollback from Valkey 7.2 to Redis OSS 7.1, even if the original source was older.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote:
ElastiCache only supports rolling back from Valkey 7.2 to Redis OSS 7.1. This is true even if you
upgraded to Valkey 7.2 from an earlier version than Redis OSS 7.1.

facts.statement: ElastiCache cross-engine upgrades using custom parameter groups require a Valkey group with the same Redis OSS static parameter values.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: If you have a custom cache parameter group applied to the existing Redis OSS replication group you wish to upgrade, you will need to pass a custom Valkey cache parameter group in the request as well. The input Valkey custom parameter group must have the same Redis OSS static parameter values as the existing Redis OSS custom parameter group.

facts.statement: The Valkey 9.1 announcement reports 2.1 million requests/second with 512-byte payloads, nine IO threads and pipeline depth ten; this is a project-reported result.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote: Valkey 9.1.0 pushes single server throughput to 2.1 million requests per second using 512-byte payloads, 9 IO threads, and a pipeline depth of 10 commands.

facts.statement: ElastiCache rollback requires associated users and user groups to use engine type REDIS.
facts.author: valkey-research

citations.quote:
Any user group and user associated with the replication group or serverless cache being rolled back
must be configured with engine type REDIS.

facts.statement: Valkey Search limits its compatibility contract to Redisearch Dialect 2 features it implements; it does not promise every Redisearch feature.
facts.author: report-revision

citations.quote: The contract applies only to Redisearch Dialect 2 with features that Valkey Search actually implements. Valkey Search may not include every feature of Redisearch.

facts.statement: Valkey Search documents rebuilding indexes from underlying hashes or JSON documents when migrating between it and Redisearch; persisted index state cannot be copied.
facts.author: report-revision

citations.quote: Redisearch RDB files cannot be loaded directly by Valkey Search, and vice versa. Migrations between the two must rebuild indexes from the underlying data (hashes or JSON documents), not by copying persisted index state.

facts.statement: Valkey governance assigns management to a Technical Steering Committee composed of repository maintainers.
facts.author: report-revision

citations.quote: The Valkey project is managed by a Technical Steering Committee (TSC) composed of the maintainers of the Valkey repository.

facts.statement: Valkey governance caps same-organization or affiliated-organization representation on its TSC at one third.
facts.author: report-revision

citations.quote: At any time, no more than one third (1/3) of the TSC members may be employees, contractors, or representatives of the same organization or affiliated organizations.

facts.statement: Redis Ltd. describes itself as setting and executing Redis’s vision; this is the vendor’s self-description.
facts.author: report-revision

citations.quote: We set the vision for Redis and execute on it.

facts.statement: Redis reports more than five times the throughput for Redis 8.6 versus Redis 7.2 in its published caching benchmark; this is a vendor claim comparing Redis releases.
facts.author: report-revision

citations.quote: Redis 8.6 in Redis Open Source: More than 5x throughput compared to Redis 7.2

facts.statement: The cited Redis 8.6 caching benchmark uses 16 cores on m8g.24xlarge, 11 I/O threads, pipeline depth 1, 2000 clients, a 1:10 SET:GET ratio, 1M keys and 1K string values.
facts.author: report-revision

citations.quote: Single node; using only 16 cores on an m8g.24xlarge instance (ARM, Graviton4); 11 io-threads; Pipeline size: 1; 2000 clients Caching use case: 1:10 SET : GET ratio; 1M keys; 1K string values

facts.statement: Redis benchmarking guidance requires comparable operations and benchmark behavior across data stores.
facts.author: report-revision

citations.quote: Finally, the benchmark should apply the same operations, and work in the same way with the multiple data stores you want to compare. It is absolutely pointless to compare the result of redis-benchmark to the result of another benchmark program and extrapolate.

facts.statement: Redis documents that WAIT improves real-world failover safety without making Redis strongly consistent.
facts.author: report-revision

citations.quote: `WAIT` does not make Redis a strongly consistent store: while synchronous replication is part of a replicated state machine, it is not the only thing needed. However in the context of Sentinel or Redis Cluster failover, `WAIT` improves the real world data safety.

facts.statement: Redis documents a possible one-second data-loss window with appendfsync everysec in a disaster.
facts.author: report-revision

citations.quote: appendfsync everysec: fsync every second. Fast enough (since version 2.4 likely to be as fast as snapshotting), and you may lose 1 second of data if there is a disaster.

findings.title: Redis takeout is strongest at the OSS 7.2 compatibility baseline

summary.text: Core workloads originating on Redis OSS 7.2 or earlier are practical Valkey migration candidates, subject to application and operations validation. Later Redis data formats make the migration a different engineering problem.

conditions.text: Pin the exact server, client, module and hosting versions before selecting a migration method.

Compatibility is bounded to the documented shared baseline. Redis CE 7.4+ file incompatibility is established; the guide does not establish a validated alternate migration for those versions. Preserve that distinction in downstream claims.
The transaction-change counterevidence matters because a client can connect successfully while error-path semantics differ. Treat connection success as one test, never the compatibility verdict.

implications.text: A pilot is a reasonable next step for shared-core workloads; a required semantic difference, unproven migration method or unacceptable recovery exposure can reverse that choice.

findings.title: Feature labels do not establish interchangeability

summary.text: Redis 8 includes richer data capabilities and Valkey has JSON/search modules; neither the shared names nor module API compatibility establish parity for a particular query, persistence image or framework.

conditions.text: Preserve the implemented-Dialect-2 boundary and index rebuild requirement whenever discussing Search compatibility. These are concrete work items, not generic cautions, and the captured rolling document must be checked against the chosen module release.

The strongest case for staying is a required integrated data feature or commercial conflict-resolution behavior whose substitute remains unproven. JSON/search availability alone neither proves equivalence nor proves a migration impossible.

gaps.text: No specific Redis Stack module, ORM, query dialect, module binary or production dataset was supplied.

implications.text: Keep a dependent workload on its existing service until its required behavior is proven on a pinned target.

findings.title: License and governance are decision inputs, not substitutes for fit

summary.text: Valkey BSD and Redis 8 AGPL/RSAL/SSPL options are materially different choices. Calling all current Redis closed source would misstate its available licensing.

conditions.text: Keep licenses version-specific. Redis 8’s AGPL option rebuts the blanket assertion that current Redis has no open-source option. Governance evidence differs: Valkey has a formal TSC policy; the Redis evidence here is a company self-description, not a formal maintainer-selection policy.

gaps.text: No legal assessment of the intended distribution model, support contract comparison or formal Redis maintainer-selection policy was evaluated.

implications.text: Evaluate governance influence, license requirements and available service support separately from application compatibility; permissive licensing can motivate a pilot without establishing lower total cost.

findings.title: Capacity and resilience need workload evidence

summary.text: Both projects publish configuration-specific performance claims. Both document durability limits, so neither a benchmark headline nor retaining the current engine settles application performance or recovery objectives.

conditions.text: Redis’s reported improvement is against Redis 7.2, not Valkey. Valkey’s reported result uses different settings. Neither provides a matched head-to-head ranking or application result. Preserve versions, workload/configuration and publisher attribution with either headline.

The Redis counterexample matters: an upgrade within Redis may offer capacity improvement, so replacement should compete against that option. This evidence does not establish the upgrade benefit for this application.

gaps.text: No workload measurement or total-cost model was run; a universal performance or cost ranking is unsupported.

implications.text: Compare a supported Redis upgrade and a Valkey pilot under the same application workload and recovery targets before crediting migration with performance or cost savings.

findings.title: Rollback is a data-path design, not just an endpoint change

summary.text: A supported forward migration does not prove reverse compatibility or recovery of writes accepted after cutover. Managed services can impose especially narrow rollback versions.

conditions.text: Preserve the provider-specific scope: ElastiCache documents the Valkey 7.2 to Redis OSS 7.1 rollback pair; this is not an upstream guarantee for Valkey 8 or 9. Returning endpoints to an old source also leaves post-cutover writes unresolved.

gaps.text: No tested reverse-transfer tool or application-specific replay/reconciliation method was established.

implications.text: Rehearse recovery of post-cutover writes and define the rollback boundary before moving durable state.

blocks.text: Valkey is a credible replacement candidate for applications using the core Redis OSS 7.2-or-earlier surface, particularly when a permissive license is valuable. Treat replacement as a versioned compatibility project: the strongest evidence concerns that shared baseline, while newer Redis persistence, data capabilities and commercial service behavior need separate proof. There is no universal winner without the workload and operating requirements.

As of the 2026-10-17 source check, Valkey’s download page lists 9.1.2 and Redis’s latest-release API returns 8.10.2. These are currency anchors, not a recommended target pair. The migration guide’s worked standalone examples use Redis 7.2.5 and Valkey 7.2.6; do not apply their commands blindly to newer major versions or hosted products.

sections.title: Separate the engine, edition and dependency boundaries

blocks.text: For a reconstructible cache using familiar core commands, a Valkey pilot is a reasonable first move. Sessions, queues, stream consumers, counters or locks deserve a higher validation bar when missing, duplicated or reordered operations affect correctness. This distinction follows from the documented asynchronous replication and persistence loss windows; the mere ability to connect a Redis client is insufficient.

Redis 7.4+ is outside the documented file-compatibility path. A logical export/import or application-mediated rebuild may be feasible, but it must account for the exact data types and changes made while copying. This research has not validated a specific tool or a universal live migration from Redis 8; retaining Redis can be the better decision when redesign or downtime exceeds the expected benefit.

Redis 8 integrates search, JSON, time series and probabilistic structures. Valkey Search and Valkey JSON also exist, so “Valkey has no JSON or search” is an unreliable comparison. More consequentially, the captured Valkey Search compatibility contract covers only implemented Redisearch Dialect 2 features, not every Redisearch feature. It requires rebuilding indexes from underlying hashes or JSON documents rather than copying persisted index state. Budget for rebuild time and validate query results, not just imported key counts. The captured READMEs/contract are rolling repository documents; confirm their applicability to the released module and hosting package selected. Module API compatibility alone does not prove a Redis Stack component can be swapped.

Redis Software Active-Active is a separate service capability based on CRDTs. A workload relying on its conflict resolution should not be mapped to ordinary Valkey asynchronous replication without a redesign and correctness proof. This is a concrete reason to stay with the existing product, or to assess another managed architecture separately from an engine swap.

Inventory commands and options, scripts/functions, transactions, modules, serialization, client/framework versions, connection pooling, retries, TLS/ACL settings and topology discovery. Exercise representative success and error paths on the selected target. For example, Valkey 8.0 changes nested MULTI/WATCH behavior to abort a transaction; connection success would not catch that semantic difference.

Consider this illustrative example, which was not executed: a client passes PING and ordinary reads, then a faulty code path sends nested MULTI inside a transaction. The Valkey 8.0 release note records transaction abortion for nested MULTI/WATCH, so a connection-only test misses a behavior the application may depend on. The lesson is to compare complete success and failure paths against the exact source and target versions; this example does not claim every transaction changes.

Include operational consumers of the protocol. Valkey’s compatibility INFO field reports redis_version:7.2.4; identify the actual engine with server_name and valkey_version when checking versions or interpreting telemetry. Check packaging as well: Valkey 9.1 moved Lua into a module, but its release notes also say the engine is statically linked by default. Do not infer that every deployment requires a separate dynamically loaded Lua library.

sections.title: Compare operating outcomes, not headline throughput

blocks.text: Both projects report performance improvements, but their headline numbers answer different questions. Valkey’s 9.1 announcement reports 2.1 million requests/second with 512-byte payloads, nine I/O threads and pipeline depth ten. Redis reports more than five times Redis 7.2 throughput for Redis 8.6 using a single-node caching workload: 16 cores on m8g.24xlarge, 11 I/O threads, pipeline depth one, 2000 clients, 1:10 SET:GET, 1M keys and 1K string values. Both are publisher-reported results. Redis’s result is evidence to evaluate an in-family upgrade, not evidence that it beats Valkey; the differing settings prevent a defensible head-to-head ranking.

Compare p95/p99 latency and throughput under the same command mix, key/value sizes, concurrency, TLS, persistence, replica topology and failure conditions. Include memory/RSS, evictions, saturation, restart and backup/rewrite behavior. Redis’s own benchmarking guidance calls for equivalent operations and benchmark behavior across stores. No workload benchmark was run here.

Recovery objectives must survive the engine change. Valkey replication is asynchronous; WAIT can reduce exposure but does not guarantee strong consistency. AOF everysec can lose roughly one second of writes in a disaster, and snapshot/rewrite work can affect latency. These are not uniquely Valkey disadvantages: Redis also documents WAIT’s consistency limit and a possible one-second loss with AOF everysec. A team using either store as durable state needs recovery tests alongside throughput tests.

Compare the complete service bill and ownership: capacity, replicas, network, backups, patching, observability, support and migration effort. Managed-service parameters and rollback rules belong to that comparison; for example, ElastiCache requires matching static parameter values when moving custom groups to Valkey. No prices, contract terms or staffing costs were supplied, so this report cannot establish savings.

sections.title: A migration should prove correctness and recoverability

blocks.text: First define acceptance thresholds and test the exact source/target packages in an isolated environment. Restore a representative backup and replay representative application traffic. Check values and types, remaining TTLs, scripts, transaction outcomes, stream pending/consumer state where used, and index/query results where used. Key counts are a useful check but cannot establish semantic equivalence. Also test client reconnection, failover, shard routing and authentication.

Select a path consistent with the verified versions. A quiesced snapshot restore trades downtime for simplicity. For a compatible cluster, the project describes adding Valkey replicas and promoting them per primary. Rehearse the full cutover: stop or fence writers, let replication catch up, verify offsets and application state, promote, redirect/reconnect clients, and watch correctness plus latency. A live replication link alone does not prove that every final write was applied.

Define rollback before cutover. Keep a tested pre-cutover recovery point and specify who owns writes at each stage. Before new writes reach the target, returning to the preserved source may be straightforward; afterward, returning to an unchanged source discards those writes unless they can be reconciled or replayed. Test that recovery path explicitly. Do not assume newer Valkey files or features can be consumed by the old Redis source.

Consider a second illustrative example, rather than an observed incident: after a fenced cutover, the new target accepts an order-status update while the preserved old source receives no further writes. Switching the application back to that unchanged source omits the update by construction. A usable rollback design therefore needs a tested way to replay or reconcile those writes, or an explicit decision to lose them. Documented forward replication and a pre-cutover snapshot do not by themselves supply that recovery path.

For hosted services, use the provider’s exact version matrix and recovery procedure. ElastiCache currently documents rollback only from Valkey 7.2 to Redis OSS 7.1, with user/user-group engine requirements. That is not evidence for an in-place rollback from Valkey 8 or 9. Keep this provider-specific constraint separate from upstream Valkey capability.

sections.title: Governance and license choice are distinct from technical fit

blocks.text: Valkey 9.1.2 declares BSD-3-Clause. Redis OSS through 7.2 remains BSD; Redis CE 7.4–7.8 uses RSAL/SSPL, and Redis 8+ adds AGPLv3 as a choice alongside those licenses. Select the terms that fit the intended use and distribution model; the presence of an AGPL option means “Redis is no longer open source” is not an accurate blanket statement about current Redis. License preference can motivate evaluation, but it does not eliminate migration work.

Valkey’s formal governance assigns management to its maintainers’ Technical Steering Committee and limits any organization or affiliated organizations to one third of TSC membership. Redis Ltd. states that it sets and executes Redis’s vision. This is a meaningful distinction for teams weighing influence and stewardship, but the Redis source is a company self-description and does not establish its formal maintainer-selection process. Neither governance model alone proves better support, availability or operating cost.

The unresolved inputs are the current Redis product/version and host; actual commands, modules and clients; cache versus authoritative-state role; data size and growth; peak traffic and hot keys; latency, availability and recovery objectives; multi-region conflict semantics; acceptable downtime; support obligations; and available migration capacity. No application benchmark, restore drill or production compatibility test was run.

Proceed to a bounded Valkey pilot when the shared command surface, licensing goals and recovery requirements fit. Keep or upgrade Redis when integrated features or commercial Active-Active behavior are required and a substitute is unproven, or when migration effort and operational risk outweigh the expected gain. Consider a Redis upgrade as a competing option when capacity is the motive; its published performance claim still needs workload validation. The practical next step is to identify the workload’s decisive dependency and prove it in an isolated pilot before committing to replacement.

brief.title: Lead with the boundary, not the brand

blocks.text: The central takeaway for platform engineers: Valkey deserves a bounded pilot for workloads on the shared Redis OSS 7.2-or-earlier surface, but Redis takeout is a compatibility and recovery decision, not an endpoint rename. Lead with that distinction; a permissive license can motivate evaluation without proving technical fit. The audience should leave able to identify the dependency that could reverse its choice.

brief.title: Build the argument in three steps

blocks.text: Start with where the case is strongest: a reconstructible cache using the shared core command surface. Then contrast two decision-changing dependencies: Redis CE 7.4+ persistence files are outside the documented compatibility path, and Redis Software Active-Active uses CRDT semantics that ordinary asynchronous replication does not replace. This progression explains why the same migration answer cannot apply to every Redis deployment.

Next, make “compatible” concrete. Existing clients can connect, yet Valkey 8.0 records changed nested MULTI/WATCH transaction behavior. Search is another useful boundary: Valkey Search exists, but its captured contract covers only implemented Redisearch Dialect 2 features and requires index rebuilding from hashes or JSON documents. These examples support testing failure paths and query results, not merely PING and key counts; the rolling module documents still require release-specific confirmation.

Close with the decision that survives cutover. In an illustrative scenario—not an observed incident—the new target accepts a write while the preserved old source stays unchanged. Switching back omits that write unless it is replayed or reconciled. Use this mechanism to connect compatibility testing to a rehearsed recovery path, then ask which validation would most likely stop this particular migration.

brief.title: Keep the strongest evidence in speaker notes

blocks.text: A source/target/write-flow sketch can explain the rollback problem more clearly than a throughput race. If showing performance claims, retain the publishers and configurations: Valkey’s 9.1 headline uses 512-byte payloads, nine I/O threads and pipeline depth ten; Redis’s 8.6 claim compares against Redis 7.2 with 1K values, eleven I/O threads and pipeline depth one. These are different tests, not a head-to-head ranking. Redis’s own upgrade is a legitimate alternative to evaluate when capacity is the motive.

Give the strongest case for staying with Redis: required integrated features or commercial Active-Active semantics may outweigh a license preference and replacement effort. Both stores document limits to WAIT and possible AOF-everysec data loss, so resilience should be tested on both sides. Valkey’s governance and BSD license are distinct benefits to assess, not proof of lower operating cost.

The evidence was captured on 2026-10-17; release listings are date anchors, not recommended targets. The migration walkthrough uses Redis 7.2.5 and Valkey 7.2.6. ElastiCache’s documented rollback pair is specifically Valkey 7.2 to Redis OSS 7.1, not a promise for newer upstream releases. Keep edition, version and provider labels beside these claims.

No application benchmark, production migration, cost model or recovery drill was run. The actual workload, modules, topology, downtime budget and recovery objectives remain unknown; the presentation can justify a validation plan, not promise savings or migration success.
